blocks.text: Some business processes take minutes or days and involve several services: onboarding a merchant (KYC check → bank verification → manual review → activation), fulfilling an order, running a video through transcoding and moderation. Any step can fail or time out; processes must survive deploys and machine crashes; and someone will ask "where is order 123 stuck?". Hand-rolling this with queues, cron jobs and status columns works at first, then turns into an unmaintainable web of retries and edge cases.

head: Approach
Good for
Breaks down when
rows: Single-step background tasks (resize image, send email)
Simple state machines with few states
Many states, timers, retries per step
You need visibility and control over the whole flow

blocks.caption: How a workflow engine survives a crash

blocks.text: The workflow function is ordinary code (`await charge(); await reserve(); await sleep('3 days'); await remind();`), but every result is recorded in an event history. After a crash, the engine replays the function against the history: completed activities return their recorded results instantly, so execution resumes exactly where it left off. Timers of days or months are just durable events.

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Workflow code must be deterministic (no random numbers, clock reads or I/O) because it's replayed. Side effects belong in activities, which are retried with their own timeouts and must be idempotent.

items: Return **202 Accepted** with a job/workflow id immediately.
Clients poll `GET /jobs/{id}`, or subscribe via SSE/WebSocket, or receive a webhook on completion.
Store progress and partial results so the UI can show "step 3 of 5".
Support cancellation as a signal to the workflow, which runs compensations.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Holding an HTTP request open for a multi-minute task. Load balancers time out, clients retry, and you get duplicates. Make it asynchronous.

items: Non-idempotent activities duplicate side effects on retry.
Huge payloads in workflow history — store blobs externally and pass references.
Unbounded retries of permanent errors — classify errors as retryable or not.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: I'd model checkout as a Temporal workflow: each step is an idempotent activity with its own timeout and retry policy, compensations run in reverse on failure, and the API returns 202 with a workflow id the client can poll.
